endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Finally, evaluate whether there are some individuals or groups who are systematically excluded from giving feedback due to language barriers or factors related to ability or access.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing machine-assisted translation in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Patient advisory boards can be leveraged to collect direct patient feedback on clarity and acceptability of translations

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether assessing language barriers in AI feedback channels changes who gives feedback or which problems get reported, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on two endorsements, a framework and a commentary, so it reflects expert judgment rather than tested effect.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Support comes from one framework (CHAI) and one commentary on machine-assisted translation, both using "should" language. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without supporting data cannot be rated, so certainty in any effect of this assessment is not estimable.

The hazard concerns patients with limited English proficiency, yet no supplied study measures whether these patients are underrepresented in AI feedback data. The translation commentary proposes patient advisory boards to gather feedback on translation clarity, but it reports no data on whether such boards reach patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should first measure the size of the gap by comparing feedback submission rates and complaint content for AI tools between patients with and without limited English proficiency. Later studies could test whether translated feedback channels, interpreter-assisted outreach, or advisory boards change participation rates and surface safety problems that English-only channels miss.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Health systems that adopt this recommendation would be acting on expert consensus alone and would need to collect their own data to learn whether their assessment reaches the patients it targets.
